scenes.narration: Watch the arrow. Before this coin finishes one lap, it has already made a full turn. By the end, it has turned twice. Keep your eye on the same coin. Now its center leaves a trail. That trail is the path we need to measure. The center stays two coin radii from the middle, so its circular path is twice one coin's circumference. But why does center travel tell us the spin? Freeze the contact. Forward motion of the center and backward motion from spinning cancel at the touching point. That is rolling without slipping. Center speed equals radius times spin speed. Across the journey, two circumferences of center travel mean two turns. Now make the obstacle three times as wide as the little coin. The center travels four small radii from the middle. One lap now produces four turns. Follow the center, not just the edge.
